newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish 96 deficit fall raises analysts' eyebrows.
newsitem.headline: Spanish 96 deficit fall raises analysts' eyebrows.

text.p: Spain's 1996 state deficit declined to 3.3 percent of gross domestic product, undershooting the government's 3.5 percent target, but analysts puzzled over the data and questioned whether the deficit could narrow further this year.
On a national account basis the 1996 deficit fell to a mere 2.45 trillion or a 3.3 percent of GDP, the Economy Ministry said in a statement on Friday.

But it also said Spain had ended 1996 with a deficit on a cash basis of 3.68 trillion pesetas, the figure bloated by a surprise shortfall discovered last July. That figure declines to 3.08 trillion pesetas when the gap isn't taken into account.
"There's a big difference between the two methods which is hard to explain even taking into account the payments in interest," said Colin Warren economist at Tokai Bank in London.

The central government public deficit on a national account basis is the one considered relevant for the Maastricht Treaty, which sets out the economic requirements that must be met to join the European single currency launch.
It takes into account accrued revenues and expenditures for a given period, while the deficit on a cash basis registers actual money movements during a given month.
In December, the director of the Spanish Treasury, Jaime Caruana, explained that the difference between the two stemmed in part from overdue interest payments only paid in 1996.
But the difference in the figures from the two accounting system increased dramatically in December from November.
In November, the deficit was 2.156 trillion pesetas on a national account basis, and 2.13 trillion on a cash basis, excluding the effect of the shortfall.
But in December, the deficit on a national account basis rose to 2.45 trillion pesetas, while on a cash basis, again excluding the effect of the shortfall, rose to 3.08 trillion.
"We now have such a big difference between the two figures which is really hard to explain," said Henrik Lumholdt, analyst at the Bank of America in Madrid.
The Economy Ministry did not give any breakdown for the December deficit on a national account basis.
It did, however, publish the breakdown of revenue and expenditure figures on a cash basis and economists said the trend was poor.
"We have a worsening trend which is making it more difficult to achieve the budget deficit this year," Lumholdt said.
He underlined that revenues had risen 3.9 percent in 1996, far beneath the initial 8.8 percent forecast. Expenditures rose 6.1 percent, well above the forecast for a modest 3.1 percent.
